Malicious PHP plugin/webshell dropped in wp-content by web server (wp2shell) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts PHP files written into wp-content/plugins or wp-content/uploads by the web-server/PHP process — the persistence/execution payload the wp2shell chain uploads after minting a rogue admin. Distinguishes attacker-dropped web shells from normal user-initiated plugin installs by anchoring on the writing process and target path. Rationale: The documented wp2shell escalation uploads a malicious plugin for code execution; a PHP file written into wp-content/plugins or the uploads dir by the PHP/web-server process is the on-disk artefact of that step. Anchored on both the target path and writing process to separate attacker drops from normal user-driven plugin installs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/wp2shell • https://www.tenable.com/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137-frequently-asked-questions-about-remote-code-execution
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1505
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator installing or updating a legitimate plugin from the WordPress dashboard (writes many .php files to wp-content/plugins)
  • Automatic plugin/theme auto-updates writing PHP during maintenance windows
  • Caching plugins (W3 Total Cache, WP Rocket) generating advanced-cache.php or object-cache.php
  • Media/gallery plugins writing helper PHP into wp-content/uploads
  • WP-CLI 'wp plugin install' run by an operator on the host
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp plugin install","wp plugin update","advanced-cache.php","object-cache.php") or FolderPath has_any ("w3-total-cache","wp-rocket"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the dropped PHP — short obfuscated files or those containing eval/base64_decode/system/assert/$_POST[ are web shells; a single .php landing directly in wp-content/uploads is almost never legitimate. Check whether the write coincides with a dashboard plugin install by a known admin. 2) CONTAIN: Quarantine the file, hash and submit it, and isolate the host if it is a web shell; revoke sessions and reset admin/DB credentials. 3) HUNT: Correlate the write time backward to author__not_in/batch/v1 exploitation in web logs and forward to web-server processes spawning shells or outbound C2, and audit wp_users for a rogue administrator created just before the drop.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "wp-content" and (FolderPath has "plugins" or FolderPath has "uploads")
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","httpd","nginx.exe","nginx","apache2")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has "wp-content" and (TargetFilePath has "plugins" or TargetFilePath has "uploads")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-cgi","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Adobe Acrobat Extension Flaw Let Malicious Sites Read WhatsApp Web Data

The Hacker News
2026-07-22 13 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched vulnerability chain in the Adobe Acrobat Chrome extension that has over 314 million users, which, if exploited, could facilitate a silent hijack of a user's WhatsApp data. The shortcoming has been codenamed HermeticReader by Guardio Labs. It's officially tracked as CVE-2026-48294 (CVSS score: 7.4), with the vulnerability

CVEsCVE-2026-48294

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable Adobe Acrobat browser extension (HermeticReader CVE-2026-48294, ver <= 26.5.2.2) on endpoint · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Vulnerable Adobe Acrobat browser extension (HermeticReader CVE-2026-48294, ver <= 26.5.2.2) on endpoint AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces managed endpoints where the Adobe Acrobat Chromium extension (ID efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj) is installed at a version at or below 26.5.2.2, which is exploitable by any malicious web page to read WhatsApp Web session data cross-origin. Article-specific because it keys on the exact extension ID and the disclosed vulnerable version ceiling, patched in 26.5.2.3. Rationale: Keys on the exact extension ID (efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj) and the disclosed vulnerable-version ceiling (<= 26.5.2.2, patched 26.5.2.3) that Guardio/Adobe published — both confirmed against BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and SOCRadar. On-disk extension-folder path is the only article behaviour EDR can actually observe; the exploit itself is intra-browser JS invisible to endpoint telemetry, and the article's two domains are researcher placeholders, so no network IOC is shippable. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/adobe-chrome-extension-flaw-let-sites-access-private-whatsapp-chats/ • https://www.securityweek.com/flaw-in-adobe-extension-with-300m-installs-enabled-whatsapp-data-theft/ • https://socradar.io/blog/adobe-acrobat-whatsapp-flaw-hermeticreader/
ATT&CKT1185 T1176.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint already auto-updated to patched build 26.5.2.3 but an old version folder lingers on disk before Chrome garbage-collects it
  • Extension staging/backup folders copied by endpoint-backup or migration tooling, showing an old version path without the extension being active
  • Corporate golden-image or roaming-profile sync replaying an outdated Extensions directory to new hosts
  • Security researchers or app-packaging teams intentionally retaining a pinned old version in a lab VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","updater.exe")   // scope to real browser/extension-updater writes, drop backup/migration tooling
Response runbook
1) Triage: On each hit, read the version folder name and confirm it is <= 26.5.2.2; open the host's Chrome/Edge extension inventory to verify the extension is enabled (not just a stale folder). 2) Contain: Force the extension to update via Chrome Web Store / enterprise policy (target 26.5.2.3+), or push an ExtensionSettings policy to update-block the vulnerable range; advise affected users that any WhatsApp Web session open during the exposure window may have been read. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the same hosts for chrome.exe/msedge.exe connections to web.whatsapp.com immediately followed by outbound POSTs to newly-observed external domains during the exposure window, and check for the extension across the fleet to size the exposure.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj"
| extend ExtVersion = extract(@"efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj\\([0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+)", 1, FolderPath)
| where isnotempty(ExtVersion)
| where parse_version(ExtVersion) <= parse_version("26.5.2.2")   // 26.5.2.3 is the patched build
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), SamplePath=any(FolderPath) by DeviceId, DeviceName, ExtVersion, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj"
| extend ExtVersion = extract(@"efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj\\([0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+)", 1, TargetFilePath)
| where isnotempty(ExtVersion)
| where parse_version(ExtVersion) <= parse_version("26.5.2.2")   // 26.5.2.3 is the patched build
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), SamplePath=any(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ExtVersion, ActingProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48294")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48294")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-48294")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,

// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04

Hackers Exploit Windmill Flaw to Read Arbitrary Server Files Without Authentication

The Hacker News
2026-07-22 17 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A high-severity security flaw impacting open-source developer platform Windmill has come under active exploitation in the wild, per VulnCheck. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-29059 (CVSS score: 7.5), a case of unauthenticated path traversal impacting Windmill's "get_log_file" endpoint ("/api/w/{workspace}/jobs_u/get_log_file/{filename}"). "The filename parameter is concatenated into

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Windmill traversal endpoint enumeration / mass file-read scanning (CVE-2026-29059) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Windmill get_log_file unauthenticated path traversal exploitation (CVE-2026-29059) · [LLM] Windmill SUPERADMIN_SECRET theft via /proc/1/environ traversal (CVE-2026-29059) · [LLM] Langflow /api/v1/validate/code unauthenticated RCE requests (CVE-2026-0770) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Langflow post-exploitation: cloud-metadata/credential theft and recon via spawned shell (CVE-2026-0770) · Suspicious browser extension installation · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Exploit Windmill Flaw to Read Arbitrary Server Files Without Authenticat
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Windmill get_log_file unauthenticated path traversal exploitation (CVE-2026-29059) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to Windmill's 'get_log_file' endpoint carrying directory-traversal sequences used to read arbitrary server files. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact vulnerable path '/api/w/{workspace}/jobs_u/get_log_file/{filename}' plus '../' and encoded variants, covering both direct Windmill endpoints and the Nextcloud proxy path called out by VulnCheck. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CVE-2026-29059 vulnerable path 'jobs_u/get_log_file' plus raw and URL-encoded traversal tokens and the specific target files (/etc/passwd, /proc) that VulnCheck observed in the wild; the endpoint string makes this Windmill-specific rather than a generic traversal template. Cross-checked SentinelOne, OSV and Field Effect confirming endpoint and payloads. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29059/ • https://osv.dev/vulnerability/CVE-2026-29059 • https://fieldeffect.com/blog/active-exploitation-windmill-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei/VulnCheck) probing the get_log_file endpoint from a known scanning subnet
  • Windmill's own UI legitimately fetching job log files (path contains 'jobs_u/get_log_file' but NO traversal tokens — excluded by the traversal clause)
  • Security researchers or internal red team validating patch status against 1.603.3
  • URL-encoded '..' appearing in a legitimate workspace or filename value that is not actually a traversal
  • WAF already blocked the request (EventOutcome=blocked) — still logged but not a successful read
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !has "Nuclei" and SourceIP !in ("<approved-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestURL and scStatus/EventOutcome for the SourceIP; a 200/206 to a get_log_file request containing '../' or '/proc/' confirms a successful arbitrary read. Check whether the instance is < 1.603.3. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF/edge, and if patch is missing, take the Windmill instance offline or gate it behind auth; rotate SUPERADMIN_SECRET and any credentials reachable via file read. 3) Hunt: search the same SourceIP for follow-on reads of /proc/1/environ (secret theft) and subsequent authenticated Bearer-token calls to Windmill job/preview APIs indicating superadmin RCE.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "jobs_u/get_log_file"
| where RequestURL has_any ("../", "..%2f", "..%252f", "%2e%2e", "/proc/", "%2fproc%2f", "/etc/passwd", "%2fetc%2fpasswd")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, EventOutcome
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Windmill SUPERADMIN_SECRET theft via /proc/1/environ traversal (CVE-2026-29059) AIExploitation High
Hunts the specific escalation step where the Windmill path traversal is aimed at /proc/1/environ (or /proc/self/environ) to read the SUPERADMIN_SECRET environment variable, which is then usable as a Bearer token for superadmin RCE via the job-preview API. Narrower and higher-severity than generic file read because this target is the direct path to full compromise. Rationale: Uses the article's precise credential-theft primitive: reading /proc/1/environ via the get_log_file traversal to obtain SUPERADMIN_SECRET (confirmed by SentinelOne and OSV). Targeting the process environ file makes this a near-zero-FP indicator of secret theft, not just recon. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29059/ • https://osv.dev/vulnerability/CVE-2026-29059
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised pentest/red-team validating the full exploit chain to prove SUPERADMIN_SECRET exposure
  • Vulnerability scanner plugin that specifically reads /proc/1/environ as its PoC check
  • Internal patch-verification tooling replaying the CVE against a staging Windmill
  • A monitoring agent path that coincidentally references 'environ' but not via the get_log_file endpoint (excluded by the endpoint clause)
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<approved-scanner-ips>") and RequestClientApplication !has "Nuclei"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm a 200/206 response to the get_log_file request containing /proc/1/environ from an external SourceIP — this means SUPERADMIN_SECRET was likely disclosed. 2) Contain: immediately rotate SUPERADMIN_SECRET and any other secrets stored in the Windmill container environment, revoke active superadmin tokens, block the SourceIP, and patch to 1.603.3+. 3) Hunt: review Windmill API logs for Bearer-token authenticated calls (especially job run/preview) from that SourceIP or new IPs after the read timestamp, indicating the stolen secret was used for RCE.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "jobs_u/get_log_file"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/proc/1/environ", "proc%2f1%2fenviron", "/proc/self/environ", "proc%2fself%2fenviron")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, EventOutcome
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| sort - lastTime
Windmill traversal endpoint enumeration / mass file-read scanning (CVE-2026-29059) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single source rapidly issuing many distinct get_log_file traversal requests — the enumeration/scanning behaviour VulnCheck saw across ~170 exposed hosts, and the post-exploitation shift from one manual file read to systematic discovery of additional targets. Threshold-based on distinct traversal paths per source in a short window. Rationale: Turns the article's observed scanning at scale (170 hosts, 24 countries) into a per-source velocity signal keyed on the get_log_file traversal path; the distinct-path count separates a probing/enumeration campaign from a one-off manual read. Threshold-based, so Sigma is intentionally omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29059/ • https://fieldeffect.com/blog/active-exploitation-windmill-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1083
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised authenticated vulnerability scanner sweeping many payload variants against the endpoint
  • Load/performance testing that replays log-fetch requests at volume
  • A single CDN/proxy egress IP aggregating many legitimate Windmill users (NAT) — tune threshold or exclude known proxy IPs
  • Bug-bounty researcher fuzzing the endpoint with a wordlist
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<approved-scanner-ips>", "<known-nat-egress-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review sampleTargets for one SourceIP — a spread of system-file paths (/etc/*, /proc/*) with 200 responses confirms active enumeration and successful reads. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the edge/WAF and confirm the instance is patched to 1.603.3+; if reads succeeded, treat secrets/config on the host as exposed. 3) Hunt: pivot on that SourceIP across all internet-facing apps for the same traversal pattern, and check whether any request reached /proc/1/environ (secret theft) or transitioned to authenticated API calls.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where RequestURL has "jobs_u/get_log_file"
| where RequestURL has_any ("../", "..%2f", "%2e%2e", "/proc/", "/etc/")
| summarize reqCount=count(), distinctPaths=dcount(RequestURL), sampleTargets=make_set(RequestURL, 20), firstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), lastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where distinctPaths >= 10   // >=10 distinct traversal targets from one source in 10m = enumeration, not a single manual read
| order by reqCount desc
source:linux.syslog jobs_u/get_log_file (*../* OR *%2e%2e* OR */proc/* OR */etc/*)
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as reqCount dc(Web.url) as distinctPaths values(Web.status) as statuses min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*jobs_u/get_log_file*") (Web.url="*../*" OR Web.url="*..%2f*" OR Web.url="*%2e%2e*" OR Web.url="*/proc/*" OR Web.url="*/etc/*") by Web.src Web.dest _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinctPaths >= 10
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - reqCount
| tstats summariesonly=false count as reqCount dc(Web.url) as distinctPaths values(Web.status) as statuses min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*jobs_u/get_log_file*") (Web.url="*../*" OR Web.url="*..%2f*" OR Web.url="*%2e%2e*" OR Web.url="*/proc/*" OR Web.url="*/etc/*") by Web.src Web.dest _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinctPaths >= 10

Langflow /api/v1/validate/code unauthenticated RCE requests (CVE-2026-0770) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated POST requests to Langflow's '/api/v1/validate/code' (exec_globals) endpoint — the vector CISA flagged as actively exploited alongside the Windmill flaw. Article-specific via the exact vulnerable endpoint and the observed payloads (id/whoami, /etc/passwd read, AWS-credential and container-metadata theft, wget/curl malware fetch). Rationale: Targets the confirmed CVE-2026-0770 vulnerable endpoint /api/v1/validate/code (SentinelOne, BleepingComputer, THN KEV writeup) — the exec_globals RCE path. POST bodies (containing __import__/subprocess) aren't always in access logs, so this is scoped as a hunting pivot on the endpoint itself; pair with UC5 for confirmed execution. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-0770/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-orders-feds-to-patch-actively-exploited-langflow-rce-flaw/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal Langflow users building/validating flows via the UI, which calls /api/v1/validate/code during normal component editing
  • CI/CD or automated flow-import pipelines that validate code blocks
  • Authorised scanner/PoC (0xBlackash / 0xgh057r3c0n GitHub PoCs) testing the endpoint
  • Health-check probes hitting the API path without a malicious body
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<internal-langflow-user-subnets>", "<approved-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: separate external SourceIPs from internal; a POST to /api/v1/validate/code from an untrusted IP against an unauthenticated/internet-facing Langflow (<= 1.4.2) is high priority. Retrieve the request body from WAF/app logs and look for __import__/subprocess/os.system. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP, restrict the endpoint behind auth, and if a body confirms code execution assume root-level host compromise — isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC5 (langflow-spawned shell/curl/wget, cloud-metadata access) on the same host to confirm successful RCE and identify what was stolen.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/validate/code"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, EventOutcome
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow post-exploitation: cloud-metadata/credential theft and recon via spawned shell (CVE-2026-0770) AIInstallation High
Confirms successful CVE-2026-0770 RCE on the host by detecting Langflow/Python-parented processes running the observed post-exploitation commands: id/whoami recon, reads of /etc/passwd and /proc/self/environ, access to AWS credentials, and SSRF to the 169.254.169.254 cloud metadata endpoint, or wget/curl second-stage downloads. Rationale: Maps the article's Langflow post-exploitation payloads verbatim — id/whoami, /etc/passwd, AWS credentials, container metadata (169.254.169.254), wget/curl second-stage downloads — to a Langflow/Python parent process chain. The 169.254.169.254 + credential-file combination under a Langflow parent is a high-fidelity confirmed-RCE signal. Corroborated by SentinelOne and CISA/BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-0770/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-orders-feds-to-patch-actively-exploited-langflow-rce-flaw/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1552.005 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow flows that intentionally shell out (curl/wget to fetch data) as part of a designed component
  • Cloud-init / SSM / instance agents that legitimately query 169.254.169.254 (excluded here by the Langflow/Python parent constraint)
  • Admin or CI running id/whoami/curl during troubleshooting under a python venv unrelated to Langflow
  • A Langflow component performing an authorised outbound HTTP call to an internal API
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "169.254.169.254" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cloud-init","amazon-ssm-agent","cloud-init-per"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain traces to the Langflow service and inspect the child command line — access to 169.254.169.254 or .aws/credentials from a web-app process is almost never benign. Check Langflow version (<= 1.4.2) and internet exposure. 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke/rotate any IAM role credentials the instance profile grants (assume IMDS creds are stolen), kill the Langflow process, and block outbound to attacker infrastructure. 3) Hunt: review outbound connections for wget/curl-downloaded second-stage payloads, new persistence (cron, systemd), and use of the stolen cloud credentials in CloudTrail (AssumeRole/GetCallerIdentity from new IPs).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "langflow" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "langflow" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","id","whoami","nc","ncat")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("169.254.169.254","/latest/meta-data",".aws/credentials","/proc/self/environ","/etc/passwd")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "langflow" or ParentProcessName has "langflow" or ParentProcessName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","id","whoami","nc","ncat")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("169.254.169.254","/latest/meta-data",".aws/credentials","/proc/self/environ","/etc/passwd")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |

    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04

logsource:

    product: windows

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:

    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:

      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

The upgrade trap: when upgrading is the wrong answer to a CVE

Aikido
2026-07-22 5 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

Upgrading to fix a CVE sounds straightforward. But the patched version often breaks your app, hasn't shipped yet, or doesn't exist. Here's why, and what actually works. Category: News

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound phishing email or URL referencing npm look-alike domain npmjs.help · [LLM] Endpoint DNS resolution or web connection to npm phishing domain npmjs.help
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Inbound phishing email or URL referencing npm look-alike domain npmjs.help AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound mail whose sender domain or embedded URL uses the typosquat domain npmjs.help, the exact lure infrastructure used to phish the npm maintainer of chalk/debug and hijack their account. Any mail touching this domain is credential-harvest phishing, not a legitimate npm communication (real npm uses npmjs.com / github.com). Rationale: Anchored on the exact IOC npmjs.help (sender domain and embedded URL), the phishing infrastructure confirmed by Sygnia/StepSecurity/Semgrep as the vector that compromised the chalk & debug maintainer account. Sentinel left blank: this tenant's provided schema exposes no Microsoft Defender for Office 365 email tables (EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo have no clean Sentinel equivalent; OfficeActivity does not carry sender/URL domain reliably). Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch blank: FDR and these sources do not ship M365 mailflow telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/npm-supply-chain-attack-september-2025/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/20-popular-npm-packages-compromised-chalk-debug-strip-ansi-color-convert-wrap-ansi • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2025/chalk-debug-and-color-on-npm-compromised-in-new-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal purple-team / phishing-simulation platform deliberately spoofing npmjs.help to test user awareness
  • A user forwarding the phishing message to the SOC or a phishing-report mailbox (original npmjs.help URL still present in EmailUrlInfo)
  • Security-newsletter or threat-intel digest whose body links out to npmjs.help as a documented IOC (matches on EmailUrl but is benign reporting)
  • Managed-detection vendor sending an advisory that embeds the IOC domain
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull every recipient of mail matching npmjs.help via NetworkMessageId; determine DeliveryAction (Delivered vs Blocked) and whether any recipient is an npm/GitHub package maintainer or CI/CD service account. 2) CONTAIN: soft-delete/quarantine the message across all mailboxes (Explorer purge), block npmjs.help at mail gateway and web proxy, and force credential reset + re-registration of MFA for any recipient who opened the link. 3) HUNT: pivot to UrlClickEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents for npmjs.help to find users who actually reached the portal; audit npm/GitHub account activity (new tokens, published package versions) for any maintainer recipient.
let lookback = 90d;
union
(EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "npmjs.help" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "npmjs.help"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, Indicator = SenderFromDomain, Source = "SenderDomain"),
(EmailUrlInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where UrlDomain =~ "npmjs.help"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, Indicator = UrlDomain, Source = "EmailUrl")
| order by Timestamp desc

(EmailUrlInfo
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where UrlDomain =~ "npmjs.help"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint DNS resolution or web connection to npm phishing domain npmjs.help AIDelivery High
Detects any host resolving or connecting to npmjs.help, the credential-harvest portal impersonating npm support in the September 2025 chalk/debug supply-chain compromise. Reaching this domain means a user clicked the lure and hit the fake 2FA/login page; there is no legitimate reason for an enterprise host to contact it. Rationale: Single hard IOC (npmjs.help) confirmed by multiple second sources as the phishing portal that harvested the maintainer's npm credentials; token-aligned domain match on network/DNS telemetry is near-zero-FP because the domain has no legitimate business use. Sysmon field DestinationHostname enumerated in two casings per Datadog case-sensitivity; Falcon DomainName is lower-cased but regex /i keeps it robust. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/npm-supply-chain-attack-september-2025/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/20-popular-npm-packages-compromised-chalk-debug-strip-ansi-color-convert-wrap-ansi • https://vercel.com/blog/critical-npm-supply-chain-attack-response-september-8-2025
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or threat researcher manually browsing npmjs.help during IOC investigation from a corporate host
  • Malware-analysis sandbox / detonation VM resolving the domain as part of automated URL detonation
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling (TIP, VirusTotal relay) performing passive DNS lookups of the IOC
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS solution logging the query as it blocks it (still worth confirming which host asked)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the host/user that initiated the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName should be a browser); confirm it is not a designated analyst/sandbox host, and check whether the request succeeded (ActionType=ConnectionSuccess vs a blocked/sinkholed response). 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host if a browser reached the live portal, block npmjs.help network-wide, and force password + MFA re-enrollment for the user, revoking any npm/GitHub personal-access tokens they hold. 3) HUNT: correlate back to EmailEvents/UrlClickEvents for npmjs.help to scope all recipients, and audit the org's npm dependency lockfiles/CI logs for installation of the compromised chalk/debug/ansi-styles versions pulled during the exposure window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "npmjs.help"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "npmjs.help"
| project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, Src = ClientIP, Indicator = Name, Source = "DNS"),
(ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "npmjs.help"
| project TimeGenerated, Host = SrcHostname, Src = SrcIpAddr, Indicator = Url, Source = "Web")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
